author: Pip Hinman
title: Health workers demand regulator stop silencing them on Palestine
content:
Hundreds of people rallied outside the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) offices on July 26 to condemn the regulatory body’s decision to implement the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

“As healthcare workers, we could not remain silent about Gaza and Palestine,” Mark Murphy, an activist with Nurses and Midwives for Palestine, told the protesters.

Healthcare workers will not be silenced by APHRA when “the health care system in Gaza has been and continues to be systematically annihilated” and hospitals are no longer places of safety or a sanctuary, but “are death traps”.

Murphy told Green Left that he had been a registered nurse for 30 years. “I’ve been a part of Nurses and Midwives for Palestine for the past two and a half years. We’re a group of rank-and-file union members who are opposed to the ongoing, brutal, racist, illegal, colonising, military occupation of sovereign Palestinian land.

“We've been showing up at events. We've been holding our own fundraisers. And we will not stop. We will not be silenced by a regulator who now deems that criticism of Israel is conflated with antisemitism.

“We have no issue with Jewish people whatsoever. In fact, we organise, we rally, we congregate with Jewish people on a regular basis.”

author: Isaac Nellist
title: India: Tens of thousands of students demand BJP education minister step down amid police violence
content:
Tens of thousands of youth and student protesters were attacked by police using tear gas and batons in India’s capital, New Delhi, on July 20, as they marched towards parliament to demand that Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resign.

More than 100 students were injured in the attacks. One student, 18-year-old Anshul Dev, told Al Jazeera the government “is treating us like terrorists and criminals”.

The youth-led protests began in May after exam papers for the National Eligibility Entrance Test (NEET) leaked online, voiding exam results and forcing more than 2 million students to re-sit.

The NEET is a high-pressure nationwide exam that screens students’ eligibility for admission to undergraduate medical programs.

Protesting students called for Pradhan’s resignation over his handling of the NEET leak, and over ongoing concerns about corruption and attacks on the public education system.

This leak is only the latest in a series of leaks that have lowered trust in the education system, which many blame Pradhan and the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government for undermining.

The NEET has been the subject of longstanding controversy, including over its centralised structure, commercialised coaching culture and the immense psychological stress placed on students.

title: Brazilian socialists confirmed for Ecosocialism 2026
content:
Brazilian socialists Sabrina Fernandes and Mariana Riscali are confirmed to speak at Ecosocialism 2026.

They will join activists from Canada, India, Malaysia, Pakistan, Philippines, Singapore the United States and Australia at this year's gathering over September 11–13 at the Albion Peace Centre in Magan-djin/Brisbane.

Under the theme “Resistance, Decolonisation, Liberation”, Ecosocialism 2026 will bring together activists to discuss pathways for overcoming capitalism.

● Riscali, from the Socialist Left Movement, a current within the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL) in Brazil. She is a member of PSOL's National Executive Committee and executive director of the Lauro Campos and Marielle Franco Foundation.

● Debbie Kilroy, an unapologetic abolitionist whose activism and work centres on dismantling the prison-industrial complex and all forms of carceral control and exile. Kilroy is a founder of Sisters Inside, the National Network of Incarcerated and Formerly Incarcerated Women and Girls and her law firm, Kilroy & Callaghan Lawyers.

● Jodie Hall, a Wakka Wakka trans woman and Digital Campaigner at Trans Justice Project. Hall is also a member of the local action group Trans Justice Meanjin.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Protests demand Pine Gap be closed
content:
Pine Gap, known as the Joint Defence Facility Pine Gap, is a prickly reminder that Australia remains annexed to the security interests of the United States, given the largely US-operated effort in Alice Springs, Central Australia.

As the late scholar of strategic studies Desmond Ball pithily remarked in 1988, it is “an espionage operation. Euphemisms should not be allowed to obscure this essential point.”

It grew out of a desire on the part of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) in 1965 to establish a remote Australian-sited ground control station intended for signals intelligence satellites. Land belonging to the Central Arrernte people was accordingly excised the following year for the site.

The decision, in typically rough fashion, was made without consultation and discussion with local residents or elders, a secret place that became what Trevor Paglen would describe as a “blank space on the map … erased from the public record.”

The facility includes some 800 personnel from the US National Security Agency (NSA), CIA, the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and such Australian agencies as the Australian Signals Directorate and Australian Federal Police.

Over the years, the base has become increasingly corporatised with a heavy American accent: Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and General Dynamics, IBM and Hewlett Packard all have a presence. A mere 10% of the constitu

author: Susan Price
title: Indonesia: Latest youth protests reveal failures of Prabowo’s ‘crony’ regime
content:
Green Left’s Peter Boyle spoke to Ignatius Mahendra Kusumawardhana from Perserikatan Sosialis (Socialist Union, PS), a left group in Indonesia, about the latest round of youth-led protests that kicked off in June in Jakarta.

In June this year, Indonesian young people took to the streets in protests over rising costs and fuel prices. What was the size and extent of these protests and what sparked them?

The immediate trigger was the fuel price hike of June 10, when the price of Pertamax [a widely used 92-octane gasoline sold by the state-owned energy company Pertamina] jumped from Rp12,300 to Rp16,250 per litre.

This came on top of a weakening rupiah and rising prices of staple goods.

On June 12, around 1,500 students — led by the student executive board of University of Indonesia (BEM UI) and joined by students from other campuses — marched in Jakarta.

Within a week, the actions spread to Bandung, Solo, Yogyakarta and cities in North and South Sumatra, with thousands besieging the Dewan Perwakilan Rakyat [House of Representatives, DPR] building, on June 19.

The scale of this wave of protests was smaller than the August 2025 revolt, which drew tens of thousands across the country; June was a student-led wave numbering in the thousands.

The protesters raised five demands: lower fuel and food prices, cut wasteful state spending and halt big-ticket programs like the free meal

author: Susan Price
title: Malaysia: Protesting Australian rare earth mining company’s deal with the Pentagon
content:
Ever since Western Australian-based Lynas Rare Earths set up the world’s largest rare earth refinery outside of China near the Malaysian city of Kuantan, it has faced strong community opposition based on well-founded concerns about the plant’s radioactive waste.

A broader coalition held a protest outside Malaysia’s parliament in Kuala Lumpur, on July 6, focusing on the company’s possible complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

A parliamentary special select committee began reviewing Lynas’ role in the United States’ defence supply chain, on July 16.

Using a pseudonym, Mikhaal, from the Malaysian Protest 4 Palestine (MP4P) coalition told Green Left: “While there is no direct link between Lynas and the Israeli military, a March 16 binding letter of intent signed between Lynas and the US Department of War puts Lynas squarely in the supply chain of the US military.

“And since the US have been supplying the Israeli military with billions of dollars worth of military aid — more so during the past three years — there is strong reason to suspect that Lynas products may be used to aid the genocide in Gaza.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Anti-CFMEU campaign wedges Vic Labor in election year
content:
With Jacinta Allan’s Labor government polling third place in the Victorian election in November, the bosses are amping up their anti-union campaign, demanding she call a royal commission to uncover “hidden” evidence of unlawfulness in the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU).

The establishment media, including the ABC, is driving the campaign against the CFMEU. Nick McKenzie, from The Age, is leading the charge on the Victorian government’s failure to “clean up” the “industry”.

Almost every day, there is another attack piece.

On July 20, McKenzie and Kieran Rooney alleged that “Labor’s signature $100 billion Big Build program had been infiltrated by criminal gangs and corrupt union and business practices” and that Allan had failed to deal with the alleged problem. McKenzie and Rooney quote others in their salacious pieces, never verifying their sources.

The fact that no CFMEU official has been convicted in Victoria does not faze them.

The few charges that were laid against organisers, such as Gerry McCrudden or First Nations organiser Joel Shackleton, appear to have stalled, either due to lack of evidence or because they were so minor.

Predictably, Labor’s defence has been weak, because it too wants to weaken the CFMEU. It has supported and defended the federal Labor government’s forced administration of the CFMEU since August 2024.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Qld gov’t, bosses plan to hammer building workers
content:
Queensland’s Liberal National Party (LNP) government is proposing to cut construction workers’ pay and conditions and restrict their right to organise as part of its attack on the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU).

The proposals, which are part of the LNP’s bid to amend the state’s Building and Construction Code, go well beyond the limits already in place under federal industrial relations laws.

Unions counter that resourcing regulators of existing industrial relations, and health and safety laws, would resolve disputes in the building industry. But their ability to mobilise their members to protect their interests against the LNP and employers’ attacks is hamstrung by the federal government’s imposition of administrators on the construction division of the CFMEU. The administrators have taken power away from the union’s delegates and removed the elected officials.

The LNP commission was set up to investigate the construction division. However, it is impacting the building industry broadly.

It is proposing a new building and construction code to replace the former Labor government’s Best Practice Industry Conditions policy, which the LNP paused soon after being elected. It wants the new code in place before negotiations on enterprise agreements begin over infrastructure building for the 2032 Olympic Games and other major infrastructure projects.

author: Pip Hinman
title: The royal commission must stop erasing Palestinians’ experiences, voices
content:
Palestinians and their supporters in Australia continue to face restrictions, accusations and exclusion, the latest example being the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion where Gaza is being discussed at length, but Palestinians are being largely excluded.

That absence did not come out of nowhere.

The Palestine solidarity movement in NSW has for months been placed under suspicion for a crime it had nothing to do with — the Bondi attack. It was an antisemitic act of terrorism against Jewish Australians and the government has a duty to investigate the attack, hold those responsible to account and protect the Jewish community.

But it has gone a lot further with sweeping restrictions on public protest, even criminalising it.

The commission’s third round of public hearings examined antisemitism and hateful speech online, in the media and in public broadcasting. The ABC and SBS were questioned about their coverage of Gaza, with claims that they focused too heavily on Gaza, portrayed Israel too negatively and gave too much space to critics of the Israeli government.

While Gillian Segal, Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, wants greater oversight, the ABC and SBS executives defended their editorial independence and complaints processes.

author: Susan Price
title: 1000 days of genocide: Sustained, organised pressure is the only option
content:
July 3 marked 1000 days since Israel launched its onslaught on Gaza. One thousand days of live-streamed slaughter. One thousand days in which the world's most powerful states have had every opportunity to intervene, and chose instead to keep arming, funding and diplomatically shielding the state carrying it out.

This is not a war we failed to see. It is a genocide we watched, in real time, on the same phones we use to order dinner.

The numbers are almost impossible to hold in the mind, which is precisely why they must be repeated until they are. More than 73,000 Palestinians killed. More than 21,000 of them children and more than 1000 of them babies who had barely begun to live. Tens of thousands more wounded, maimed, amputated. Nearly 60,000 children orphaned.

A ceasefire was declared in October 2025, and still the killing has not stopped: The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund says a Palestinian child has been killed in Gaza on average almost every day since. Ninety per cent of Gaza's buildings are destroyed. A population of two million people repeatedly displaced, starved and bombed again on the land they were told to flee to for safety.

This is what 1000 days of "restraint", "self-defence" and "targeted operations" looks like.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Telstra outage shows communications network should be publicly owned
content:
Telstra’s July 8 network outage cut millions of people off from communication, disrupted triple zero services and affected public transport, especially in regional areas.

About 1700 people were left stranded at Naarm/Melbourne’s Southern Cross Station and thousands of others faced delays as the outage shut down Victoria’s V/Line regional train services communications network.

In addition to phone and internet services going down, electronic payment systems and other systems that rely on mobile networks were affected.

The outage was reportedly caused by timekeeping systems that Telstra Chief Financial Officer Michael Ackland said are “critical to the way all networks run”. The ABC reported that government agencies and academics had warned Telstra for years that it was vulnerable to this issue, but nothing was done.

The failure of the country’s largest telecommunication company brought to mind the similar 2023 Optus network outage, which affected about 10 million people.

Two-thirds of the population have been directly affected by the two outages in the past three years, highlighting just how vulnerable these systems are. These disruptions go beyond simple inconvenience to have serious economic effects, with costs reaching into the billions.

How then were Telstra and Optus allowed to fail? These vital services should be among our most secure, but they have been consistently

author: Pip Hinman
title: Islamophobia is the greater racist problem today
content:
Islamophobia is a bigger problem than antisemitism in Australia today, but government agencies and the mainstream media would have you think the opposite.

Since the Bondi terror attack ast year, the Islamophobia Register Australia reported a huge 740% spike in hate incidents.

Even the conservative Centre for Independent Studies said that while Israel’s standing is at a “low ebb”, the public’s warmth towards Jewish Australians is “generally encouraging”. It said while there was “a perception” of increasing antisemitism, especially among older Australians, “in terms of attitude alone, Australia does not have a particular problem with antisemitism”.

The study found that Australians are much more likely to be negative towards Muslims: About 30% have negative feelings towards Muslims, while only 12% have negative feelings towards Jews. Ten percent have an “extremely negative” view of Muslims compared to just 3% towards Jews.

The brutal bashing of a Muslim father of three in late June has prompted the Australian Federation of Islamic Councils (AFIC) to again call on the federal government and media organisations to commit to a serious national response to Islamophobia.

author: Alex Bainbridge
title: Photos: Trans rights counter protesters dwarf transphobic rally
content:
More than 1000 protesters rallied for trans rights and against racism in Magan-djin/Brisbane on July 12 dwarfing a transphobic gathering of a couple of hundred people the same day.

The transphobic gathering was initially advertised as featuring Pauline Hanson but, on the day, her One Nation colleague Malcolm Roberts took her place.

Controversially, Queensland Greens co-founder Drew Hutton spoke on the transphobic platform. Greens MP Michael Berkmann spoke at the counter rally and explicitly distanced the Queensland Greens from Hutton and the transphobic rally.

Large numbers of police kept the two protests apart, however, Riff Raff radical marching band staged a joyful, musical "drown out hate" street parade on George Street near the transphobic action.
